Summary: Roman emperor from AD 361 to 363 who had been raised Christian and then publicly returned to traditional pagan religion, earning the name 'the Apostate' from Christian writers. Key work: Against the Galileans.
KeyPoints: Against the Galileans argues against Christian teaching, engaging the Gospel accounts and claims about Jesus, his apostles, and the early church; Julian acknowledges Jesus as a historical founder and the Gospels as Christian scriptures while disputing Christian interpretations, including the divinity of Jesus; His work confirms from a hostile imperial source which Christian texts and claims were central in the 4th century
